name: Ludic fallacy
statement: The ludic fallacy is Nassim Taleb's charge that studying chance through games and dice misleads, because real uncertainty hides the rules as well as the odds.
meaning: Taleb's glossary defines it as 'the manifestation of the Platonic fallacy in the study of uncertainty; basing studies of chance on the narrow world of games and dice', and adds that 'A-Platonic randomness has an additional layer of uncertainty concerning the rules of the game in real life'. In a casino the probabilities are fixed by the house, bounded and computable. Outside it the distribution is unknown, the payoffs can be unbounded, and the rules can change while the game is running. Taleb writes that he intended to tell the symposium he should not be speaking at a casino, because it had nothing to do with uncertainty. The complaint is aimed at models and at the way probability is taught. It is not a claim about a measurable tendency in individuals. Chapter 9, the later section 'Ludic Fallacy Redux' and the glossary, which are the passages read for this entry, name no experiment and report no data beyond one casino anecdote. That places the ludic fallacy among criticisms of method rather than among effects with an effect size. The question that has been measured is narrower: whether laboratory gambles capture anything that survives outside the laboratory.

origin.where: The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable
origin.note: Chapter 9 is titled 'The Ludic Fallacy, or The Uncertainty of the Nerd'. Taleb writes that he was invited by a think tank sponsored by the United States Defense Department to a brainstorming session on risk in Las Vegas, that the organisers 'symbolically picked a major casino as a venue', and that he prepared his talk 'on five restaurant napkins, some stained' to discuss 'a new phrase I coined for the occasion: the ludic fallacy'. The book returns to it in a later section called 'Ludic Fallacy Redux', which lists the chance setups he has in mind: random walk, dice throwing, coin flipping, the digital heads or tails expressed as 0 or 1, and Brownian motion. He calls the randomness those produce protorandomness. The text quoted here was read as a scan of the Penguin Books printing, whose copyright page reads 'First published in the United States of America by The Random House Publishing Group 2007', 'First published in Great Britain by Allen Lane 2007', 'Published in Penguin Books 2008' and 'ISBN: 978-0-141-90620-1'. That printing carries the first-edition text; the phrase 'On Robustness and Fragility' does not occur in it.

evidence: Taleb's support in the passages read is a single anecdote. He reports that the four largest losses incurred or narrowly avoided by the casino hosting the symposium fell outside its models: around $100 million when an irreplaceable performer in its main show was maimed by a tiger, a thwarted attempt by a disgruntled contractor to dynamite the building, an employee who hid mandatory tax forms in boxes under his desk for years, and the kidnapping of the owner's daughter. He then offers 'a back-of-the-envelope calculation' under which these off-model hits 'swamp the on-model risks by a factor of close to 1,000 to 1'. He does not name the casino, though he names the show as Siegfried and Roy. Three of the four losses carry no figure, and the fine for the tax forms is 'an undisclosed amount'. The ratio is his own arithmetic on sums he does not print. What has been measured is the reliability of the game-like tasks themselves. Pedroni and colleagues gave six incentivised behavioural elicitation methods to 1,507 healthy adults recruited between 20 and 36 years of age, 746 in Basel and 761 in Berlin, among them the Holt and Laury gambles, the balloon analogue risk task, the Columbia card task, a marbles task, multiple price lists and adaptive lotteries. The share of participants classified as risk averse ran from 100% on the balloon task to 21% on the Columbia card task, and 88% switched from risk averse to risk seeking or the reverse at least once across the six methods. Rank-order correlations between methods were all positive, with a minimum Spearman correlation of 0.06, a maximum of 0.34 and a median of 0.11. Only 13% of participants showed the same risk preference on all six. Fitting cumulative prospect theory to three of the methods did not rescue the picture: median loss aversion came out at 0.43 on the Columbia card task, against 1.36 on the price lists and 1.64 on the adaptive lotteries. Frey and colleagues analysed the same 1,507 participants across 39 risk-taking measures drawn from three traditions, self-reported propensity, incentivised behavioural tasks, and reported frequencies of real risky activities. Correlations between behavioural and propensity measures had a posterior mode of 0.06, with a 95% highest-density interval of 0.05 to 0.06. Correlations among the behavioural measures themselves averaged 0.08, against 0.20 among the propensity measures and 0.18 among the frequency measures. In a retest subsample of 109 people six months later, propensity measures averaged 0.68 and frequency measures 0.65, while behavioural measures averaged 0.46. A bifactor model accounted for 31% of the variance, of which a general factor of risk preference took 61%, and that factor explained little to no variance in the behavioural tasks. A stricter version kept 13 of the 39 measures, accounted for 53% of the variance, and in the authors' words 'excluded all behavioral measures'. Lönnqvist and colleagues ran the comparison directly at Bonn with 232 subjects between December 2007 and February 2008. The Holt and Laury lottery task and the general risk factor extracted from the questionnaire were uncorrelated, at a Spearman correlation of -0.04, p > .10. Of those 232, 44 returned on 16 March 2009, and in that retest the questionnaire factor held at 0.780, p < .001, while the lottery task reached only 0.258, p = 0.095. The questionnaire factor predicted how much subjects sent in a trust game, at 0.231, p = 0.013; the lottery task did not, at 0.151, p = 0.107. Dohmen and colleagues put the same contest to the field. Their survey covered 22,019 individuals in 11,803 households in the 2004 wave of the German Socio-Economic Panel, and their validation experiment interviewed a representative sample of 450 adults at home between 9 June and 4 July 2005, each choosing across 20 rows between a safe sum and a lottery paying 300 euros or nothing with equal probability. The single general question about willingness to take risks was the only measure that predicted every behaviour they examined significantly and with the expected sign, across traffic offences, portfolio choice, smoking, occupational choice, sport and migration. The hypothetical lottery measure was not significantly correlated with self-employment, smoking or migration, and predicted public sector employment with the wrong sign. Laboratory lotteries are not useless. Anderson and Mellor, using the Holt and Laury task with adults aged 18 to 87, report risk aversion negatively and significantly associated with cigarette smoking, heavy drinking, being overweight or obese, and seat belt non-use. Levitt and List set out the general case for caution, arguing that laboratory behaviour is influenced 'not just by monetary calculations, but also by at least five other factors': moral and ethical considerations, the nature and extent of scrutiny by others, the context the decision is embedded in, self-selection of the individuals deciding, and the stakes of the game.

examples.tag: The risk register with a fixed list on it
examples.text: A firm assigns a probability to each item on its list of things that could go wrong and reports the total. Nothing in that calculation covers the event missing from the list, or the rules changing while the list is in use.

examples.tag: Probability taught with dice and cards
examples.text: A course sets out chance using equipment whose odds are fixed by its manufacture. The learner leaves with a method that works wherever the distribution is known, and the cases that hurt are the ones where the distribution is the unknown.

examples.tag: The contract that enumerates its own failures
examples.text: A supplier and a buyer list the ways the arrangement could fail and price each one. What remains is the part neither could name, and it is not zero merely because nobody wrote it down.

replication.headline: No test of the ludic fallacy was found. It is a criticism of how uncertainty is modelled and taught, and nobody appears to have turned it into a claim about people that could pass or fail.
replication.detail: Testing it would mean fixing what the claim predicts and about whom. Taleb's target is a model, so the nearest testable forms are whether training on games and dice leaves people worse at judging real uncertainty than some comparison training, or whether risk models calibrated on game-like assumptions miss losses at the rate he suggests. Neither design was found in the searches recorded under limits, and Taleb reports no baseline against which either could be scored. The nearest measured question is whether game-like laboratory tasks measure a stable thing. On that, the numbers favour his suspicion of the tasks. Six incentivised elicitation methods given to the same 1,507 people agreed at a median rank correlation of 0.11, and 88% of participants changed category at least once across them. Across 39 measures in the same sample, behavioural tasks correlated with self-reported propensity at 0.06 and with each other at 0.08. The same data cut the other way for stated preferences. Self-report measures converged at 0.20, held a six-month retest reliability of 0.68, and yielded a general factor of risk preference that retested at 0.85 and generalised to reported real-world activities such as smoking. What looks fragile is the laboratory gamble, which is the closest thing psychology has to Taleb's casino, rather than the measurement of risk preference as such.

limits: Nothing here tests the fallacy. The search for an empirical study of it was run on 21 September 2026 and covered Crossref, Europe PMC, arXiv and general web search. Europe PMC returns two records for the phrase, a 2020 Frontiers in Psychology piece on the practice of experimental psychology and a 2023 Frontiers in Neuroergonomics piece on normative uncertainty, and neither is a study of human subjects. arXiv returns none. Crossref was queried by title and by bibliographic string, and none of the 200 highest-ranked records on either query has the phrase in its title. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar could not be searched. OpenAlex answered 429 with a message that the free daily budget shared across the requesting network was exhausted, and Semantic Scholar answered 429 as rate-limited, both on 21 September 2026. Taleb's casino figures cannot be checked: the venue is unnamed, the amounts beyond the first are withheld, and the 1,000-to-1 ratio is his own estimate. The elicitation results describe young adults, mostly students, choosing over modest stakes, and Pedroni's sample was recruited between 20 and 36 years of age. The Frey figures quoted as averages are posterior modes from Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, and the intervals around them are 95% Bayesian highest-density intervals rather than frequentist confidence intervals. Two of the figure sets were read in working-paper form rather than as published. The Lönnqvist figures come from SOEPpapers 370 of March 2011, and the published 2015 article's abstract calls the two measures 'at best only weakly correlated' where the working paper calls them uncorrelated, so the -0.04 belongs to the working paper. The Dohmen figures come from IZA Discussion Paper 1730 of September 2005, and the 2011 article was not obtained, so agreement between the two versions was not checked. Three papers could not be read in full on 21 September 2026. Dohmen and colleagues 2011 is indexed as bronze open access at its publisher, and the publisher's own PDF, the Wiley landing page and the Wiley text-mining endpoint all refused the request, the first two with a bot challenge returning HTTP 403 rather than a paywall; the Maastricht and Munich repository records and the CORE record hold metadata and no file. Lönnqvist and colleagues 2015 is closed at Elsevier, and the Lund University record carries an abstract and no file. Anderson and Mellor 2008 is closed at Elsevier, so its figures here come from the abstract at PubMed together with the William and Mary working paper, which is cited separately below. Levitt and List concern social preference games rather than risk, and their argument is analytic rather than a measurement of the lab-field gap.
misreadings: The dialogue everyone quotes is read backwards. Taleb stipulates a fair coin, says he flips it ninety-nine times and gets heads each time, and asks the odds of tails on the next throw. Dr John says one half; Fat Tony says 'no more than 1 percent, of course', because 'The coin gotta be loaded. It can't be a fair game.' That looks like the gambler's fallacy, and Taleb's own parenthetical gloss is the opposite: 'It is far more likely that your assumptions about the fairness are wrong than the coin delivering ninety-nine heads in ninety-nine throws.' The exchange is about a premise, not about a sequence. The second error is to file the ludic fallacy with the cognitive biases and expect it to have an effect size. It was coined as a criticism of models and of teaching, and showing that a model omits something is not the same as showing that people commit an error. A third error reads it as a rejection of probability theory. Taleb's complaint is about applying machinery built for known odds where the odds are unknown, and his glossary treats the bell curve as 'the application of the ludic fallacy to randomness' rather than treating calculation itself as the problem. The elicitation literature is also claimed as vindication more broadly than it supports. It shows that incentivised laboratory gambles disagree with each other and predict poorly. It also shows that asking people a plain question about their willingness to take risks works better, which is not an argument that risk preference cannot be measured.

sources.text: Taleb, N. N. (2007). The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable. Read as the scanned full text at the Internet Archive, an open upload rather than a lending copy, whose copyright page gives Random House 2007, Allen Lane 2007, Penguin Books 2008 and ISBN 978-0-141-90620-1. Chapter 9, the 'Ludic Fallacy Redux' section and the glossary supply the definition, the coinage, the casino anecdote and the coin dialogue.

Pedroni, A., Frey, R., Bruhin, A., Dutilh, G., Hertwig, R., & Rieskamp, J. (2017). The risk elicitation puzzle. Nature Human Behaviour, 1(11), 803-809. Read as the author copy of the article PDF hosted at gwern.net, and every figure quoted was taken from its text.

Frey, R., Pedroni, A., Mata, R., Rieskamp, J., & Hertwig, R. (2017). Risk preference shares the psychometric structure of major psychological traits. Science Advances, 3(10), e1701381. Figures read from the JATS full text at Europe PMC, PMC5627985. The publisher PDF that the open-access indexes point to returned a bot challenge on 21 September 2026.

Lönnqvist, J.-E., Verkasalo, M., Walkowitz, G., & Wichardt, P. C. (2011). Measuring Individual Risk Attitudes in the Lab: Task or Ask? An Empirical Comparison. SOEPpapers on Multidisciplinary Panel Data Research No. 370, Berlin, March 2011. The sample sizes and correlations quoted here were read from this working paper at DIW Berlin. The EconStor copy of the same file returned HTTP 503 on 21 September 2026.

Lönnqvist, J.-E., Verkasalo, M., Walkowitz, G., & Wichardt, P. C. (2015). Measuring individual risk attitudes in the lab: Task or ask? An empirical comparison. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, 119, 254-266. The published version of the work above. Not obtained on 21 September 2026: closed at Elsevier, with the Lund University record carrying an abstract and no file. That abstract was read, and it calls the two measures 'at best only weakly correlated'.

Dohmen, T., Falk, A., Huffman, D., Sunde, U., Schupp, J., & Wagner, G. G. (2005). Individual Risk Attitudes: New Evidence from a Large, Representative, Experimentally-Validated Survey. IZA Discussion Paper No. 1730, September 2005. Sample sizes, the lottery design and the predictive comparison were read from this paper.

Dohmen, T., Falk, A., Huffman, D., Sunde, U., Schupp, J., & Wagner, G. G. (2011). Individual risk attitudes: measurement, determinants, and behavioral consequences. Journal of the European Economic Association, 9(3), 522-550. The published version of the work above. Indexed as bronze open access, and still not obtained on 21 September 2026: the publisher PDF at Oxford Academic and the Wiley landing page both returned a bot challenge with HTTP 403, the Wiley text-mining endpoint returned HTTP 400, and the Maastricht, Munich and CORE repository records hold metadata and no file. The figures above therefore come from the 2005 working paper.

Anderson, L. R., & Mellor, J. M. (2008). Predicting health behaviors with an experimental measure of risk preference. Journal of Health Economics, 27(5), 1260-1274. Closed at Elsevier and not obtained on 21 September 2026. Read as the abstract at PubMed, PMID 18621427, which gives the age range 18 to 87 and the four significant associations but no sample size.

Anderson, L. R., & Mellor, J. M. (2008). Predicting Health Behaviors with an Experimental Measure of Risk Preference. College of William and Mary Department of Economics Working Paper No. 59, September 2007, revised April 2008. The working paper behind the article above, and the source of counts the published version could not be read for: 1,094 subjects took part in Williamsburg, Virginia, 1,091 completed all ten lottery choices, and the models run on a maximum of 978 observations, with a mean subject age of 45.35 years.

Levitt, S. D., & List, J. A. (2007). What Do Laboratory Experiments Measuring Social Preferences Reveal About the Real World? Journal of Economic Perspectives, 21(2), 153-174. Full text read as a PDF copy of the JSTOR scan.
